course.title: Storage and Consistency
course.description: Every system-design diagram ends in a box labelled "DB", and every hard question is hiding in that box. What happens to a write if the power fails halfway through it? How can a database take 100,000 writes a second on disks that hate random writes? How do two users edit the same row without one silently erasing the other? How do three replicas agree when the network between them is cut? And how do two databases commit "both or neither"? This module builds each answer in miniature: the write-ahead log, the LSM tree, optimistic locking, MVCC, CRDTs, vector clocks, leases and two-phase commit. They are small enough to fit in one file each, and they are the same ideas you will find inside PostgreSQL, RocksDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, etcd and Kafka.

lessons.title: Storage and Consistency
lessons.explanation:
# 13 · Storage and Consistency

Every system-design diagram ends in a box labelled "DB", and every hard
question is hiding in that box. What happens to a write if the power
fails halfway through it? How can a database take 100,000 writes a second
on disks that hate random writes? How do two users edit the same row
without one silently erasing the other? How do three replicas agree when
the network between them is cut? And how do two databases commit "both or
neither"? This module builds each answer in miniature: the write-ahead
log, the LSM tree, optimistic locking, MVCC, CRDTs, vector clocks,
leases and two-phase commit. They are small enough to fit in one file
each, and they are the same ideas you will find inside PostgreSQL,
RocksDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, etcd and Kafka.

## The mental model

### 1 · Durability is a log you can replay

A disk only promises that data has landed once a flush (`fsync`) of it
has returned, and flushing one sequential file is far cheaper than
flushing pages scattered across the data files. So a database appends
every change to a **write-ahead log**, flushes it, and updates its real
data structures later. After a crash it replays the log. A
transaction becomes real at exactly one moment: when its COMMIT record is
durable.

```
BEGIN t1 | SET t1 a 1 | SET t1 b 2 | COMMIT t1 | BEGIN t2 | SET t2 c 3 ✂ crash
                                    └── t1 survives       └── t2 never happened
```

A crash can only tear the last record. A broken record with good ones
after it is not a crash, it is corruption, and recovery must refuse
rather than guess.

### 2 · Turn random writes into sequential ones (LSM)

```
put/delete ──► memtable (sorted, in memory)
                  │ full
                  ▼ flush (write once, never modify)
               run 3  (newest)    get: memtable → run 3 → run 2 → run 1
               run 2              first hit wins, even a tombstone
               run 1  (oldest)
                  │ compaction: merge runs, newest wins, drop dead entries
```

LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase and ScyllaDB all work this way. Writes
are cheap appends; reads may check several runs (bloom filters, module 11,
let them skip most); compaction pays the cleanup bill in the background.
A delete cannot remove anything from an immutable run, so it writes a
**tombstone** that shadows the older value.

| | B-tree (PostgreSQL, InnoDB) | LSM tree (RocksDB, Cassandra) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| write | update a page in place | append to memtable, flush whole runs |
| read | one tree walk | memtable + several runs (bloom filters help) |
| where writes cost extra | a whole page rewritten for a small change | the same data rewritten by each compaction |
| good for | read-heavy, predictable read latency | write-heavy, time series, logs |

### 3 · Concurrency without waiting: versions

**Optimistic locking**: read a row with its version, compute, write back
only if the version has not changed (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND
version = ?`). On a conflict, re-read and recompute. Good when conflicts
are rare; under heavy contention the retries waste work and a real lock
is better.

**MVCC** keeps every committed version stamped with its commit
timestamp. A transaction reads the snapshot at its start timestamp, so
readers never block writers and writers never block readers. At commit,
"first committer wins": if a key you wrote was committed by someone else
after your snapshot, you abort.

```
x:  (ts 1, "old")  (ts 3, "new")
tx started at ts 2 reads "old"  ← forever, however many commits follow
```

| isolation level | what it still allows |
| --- | --- |
| read committed | the same query returning different rows twice in one transaction |
| snapshot isolation (MVCC) | write skew: two transactions read the same rows and write different ones |
| serializable | nothing: it behaves as if transactions ran one at a time |

### 4 · Replicas disagree; decide how they converge

When replicas accept writes during a network partition (the "A" choice
in CAP), they will diverge. Three tools, from simplest to richest:

- **Last-writer-wins**: keep the write with the higher timestamp, ties
  broken by node id. Simple, but a concurrent write is silently lost,
  and clocks on different machines drift.
- **CRDTs**: data types whose merge is commutative, associative and
  idempotent, so replicas converge whatever order gossip arrives in. A
  G-counter gives each node its own slot and merges by per-node max.
- **Vector clocks**: one counter per node. They answer "did x happen
  before y, or did neither see the other?" Concurrent versions are kept
  as siblings for the application to merge (Dynamo's shopping cart).

```
{a:2, b:1} vs {a:2, b:3}  → BEFORE      (every counter <=, one <)
{a:3, b:1} vs {a:2, b:3}  → CONCURRENT  (some <, some >)
```

### 5 · Agreement: leases and atomic commit

A **lease** is a lock that expires, so a dead leader frees it without
anyone noticing the death. Because a paused leader does not know its
lease ran out, every lease carries an increasing **fencing token**, and
storage refuses writes with a token lower than the highest it has seen.

**Two-phase commit** makes several databases commit together: prepare
everyone (a YES is a durable promise), log the decision, then tell
everyone. The decision record in the coordinator's log is the commit
point; everything after it can be retried.

```
coordinator          p1          p2
   │── prepare ─────►│           │
   │── prepare ─────────────────►│
   │◄─ YES ──────────│◄─ YES ────│
   │ log "COMMIT"   ← point of no return
   │── commit ──────►│── commit ►│
   │ log "DONE"
```

2PC blocks: a participant that voted YES holds its locks until it hears
the decision. That is why services that cannot wait use sagas (module
12) and why consensus systems (Raft, Paxos) replicate the coordinator
itself.

## The details that bite

1. **Retry the whole read-modify-write, not just the write.** Re-sending
   a value computed from stale data is the lost update you were trying to
   prevent (exercise 01).
2. **Never reset a version.** Deleting a row and restarting its version
   at 0 lets an old writer's version match again (ABA). Keep a tombstone
   with a higher version (exercise 01).
3. **Apply a transaction at its COMMIT record, not as you read its
   operations**, and apply them in commit order, not begin order
   (exercise 02).
4. **Only the last record can be torn.** Ignoring a broken line in the
   middle of a log silently loses data; refuse with the line number
   (exercise 02).
5. **Deletes write tombstones.** Removing the key from the memtable lets
   the older run's value come back (exercise 03).
6. **Compact oldest first, then drop tombstones** — and only when every
   older run is part of the merge (exercise 03).
7. **`>` versus `>=` on timestamps.** A snapshot at ts 2 sees commits
   with ts <= 2; a conflict is a commit with ts > startTs (exercise 04).
8. **Garbage collection must keep the newest version at or below the
   horizon**; that is the one the oldest snapshot is reading
   (exercise 04).
9. **Merge with max, not plus.** Gossip repeats; an additive merge counts
   the same increments twice (exercise 05).
10. **Ties need a global tie-break.** "Keep mine" on equal timestamps
    leaves replicas disagreeing forever (exercise 05).
11. **Compare vector clocks over the union of nodes**, with missing
    counters as 0, and check BOTH directions before saying BEFORE
    (exercise 06).
12. **An expired lease is gone at exactly `acquiredAt + ttl`**, and it
    cannot be renewed back to life (exercise 07).
13. **Fence the storage, not the leader.** Only the store can reject a
    deposed leader's late write (exercise 07).
14. **Log the 2PC decision before the first commit message**, and after
    that never change it; failures only delay delivery (exercise 08).

## Cheat table

| problem | tool | real-world home |
| --- | --- | --- |
| survive a crash | write-ahead log + replay | PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL redo log, Kafka |
| fast writes on disk | LSM tree | RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB |
| two editors, one row | optimistic locking (versions / ETags) | JPA `@Version`, DynamoDB conditional writes, HTTP `If-Match` |
| readers vs writers | MVCC snapshots | PostgreSQL, Oracle, InnoDB |
| replicas merging counters | CRDT (G-counter, PN-counter) | Riak, Redis CRDTs, collaborative editors |
| detecting concurrent writes | vector clocks / version vectors | Dynamo, Riak, Voldemort |
| one active leader | lease + fencing token | etcd, ZooKeeper, Kubernetes Lease |
| commit across databases | two-phase commit | XA transactions, Spanner (2PC over Paxos) |

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-versioned-writes.java` | ★☆☆ | optimistic locking with versions, tombstones and a retry loop |
| 02 | `02-write-ahead-log.java` | ★★☆ | crash recovery from a write-ahead log, torn writes and corruption |
| 03 | `03-lsm-tree.java` | ★★☆ | a memtable, sorted runs, tombstones, compaction and range scans |
| 04 | `04-mvcc-snapshots.java` | ★★★ | MVCC snapshot reads, first-committer-wins and version GC |
| 05 | `05-crdt-merge.java` | ★☆☆ | a G-counter and a last-writer-wins register that always converge |
| 06 | `06-vector-clocks.java` | ★★☆ | vector clocks and sibling reconciliation |
| 07 | `07-leader-lease.java` | ★★☆ | leader election with leases and fencing tokens on an injected clock |
| 08 | `08-two-phase-commit.java` | ★★★ | a two-phase commit coordinator with a decision log and recovery |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows. Exercises
01–04 are one machine; 05–08 are several. If you have done modules 11
(quorums, partitioning) and 12 (outbox, sagas), notice how 02 is the
same log as the outbox relay, and 08 is the all-or-nothing that a saga
gives up on purpose.

---

**Done with the system-design block?** Read the guide that ties modules
09–13 together into whole designs. **Next:** `astraupskill/03-SYSTEM-DESIGN.md`

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** optimistic locking · versions · compare-and-set · lost updates  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Two people edit the same cart. Finish VersionedStore so neither can
silently overwrite the other. get returns (value, version); an unknown
key is (null, 0). put(key, value, expected) writes only if the
current version equals expected, then returns version + 1; otherwise
it throws ConflictException naming the key and changes nothing.
delete(key, expected) leaves a TOMBSTONE (null value, version + 1),
so versions never restart; deleting a key with no value is an
IllegalStateException (checked before the version).
update(key, change, maxAttempts) is the client loop: read, apply
change to the value read, put with the version read; on a conflict
start over; return the attempt that succeeded (1-based), or after
maxAttempts conflicts rethrow the last ConflictException.

    put("cart", "tea", 0)  → 1        put("cart", "cake", 0)  → Conflict
    delete("cart", 1)      → 2        get("cart") → (null, 2)

hint: a retry must call change again on the fresh value.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
Optimistic locking takes no lock while you think: you read a value
together with its version, compute, and write back "only if the
version is still the one I read". That last step is a compare-and-set
(in SQL: UPDATE ... SET v = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND
version = ?, then check the row count). A mismatch means somebody
wrote in between, and the right move is to re-read and recompute,
never to write your stale result anyway: that is the lost update.
update() is that loop: read, apply the change to the FRESH value,
compare-and-set, and give up after maxAttempts by rethrowing the last
conflict. The classic wrong turn is computing the new value once and
retrying only the put, which re-submits a value built from old data.
The tombstone is the subtle part. If delete removed the entry, the
version would restart at 0, and a writer still holding version 2
from before the delete could succeed once the key is recreated and
bumped back to 2 (the ABA problem). Keeping the entry with a null
value and a bumped version makes versions monotonic per key, so a
version number can never mean two different states.

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** write-ahead log · crash recovery · commit records · torn writes  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

The store crashed; all that survived is its write-ahead log. Write
recover(log) to rebuild the key-value state. Records (single spaces):
"BEGIN tx", "SET tx key value", "DEL tx key", "COMMIT tx", "ABORT tx".
A transaction's SET/DEL take effect, in log order, only when its
COMMIT is read; aborted and never-committed ones leave no trace. DEL
of an absent key is fine. A line that does not parse (unknown verb,
wrong field count, an empty field) is a TORN WRITE if it is the last
line: ignore it. Anywhere else it is corruption: IllegalStateException
whose message contains "line N" (1-based). Also corruption: any record
for a transaction that is not open (never begun, already committed or
aborted), and BEGIN of a transaction that is already open.

    BEGIN t1, BEGIN t2, SET t1 k a, SET t2 k b, COMMIT t2, COMMIT t1
                                                   → {k=a}
    BEGIN t1, SET t1 a 1, COMMIT              → {}  (torn COMMIT)

hint: buffer each open transaction's operations until its COMMIT.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
A database appends every change to a log and forces it to disk BEFORE
touching its data files; after a crash it rebuilds state by replaying
the log. The rule that makes this atomic is that only the COMMIT
record makes a transaction real. So replay keeps a buffer of pending
operations per open transaction and applies a transaction's buffer,
in order, at the moment its COMMIT line is read. Begin order does not
matter, commit order does: two transactions that wrote the same key
land in the order they committed. ABORT and "never committed" are the
same outcome: the buffer is dropped.
The classic wrong turn is applying SET lines as they are read; then a
crash halfway through a transaction leaves half of it in the data.
The other is treating every unparsable line alike. A crash can only
tear the LAST write, so a broken last line is expected and ignored
(if it was the COMMIT, that transaction simply did not commit). A
broken line with valid lines after it cannot come from a crash: that
is corruption, and silently skipping it would lose data, so recovery
refuses with the line number. A record for a transaction that is not
open is corruption of the same kind.

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** LSM tree · memtable flush · tombstones · compaction  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Build the storage engine behind RocksDB and Cassandra in miniature.
Finish Lsm: put and delete write into the memtable (delete writes a
TOMBSTONE, Optional.empty()); when the memtable then holds
memtableLimit distinct keys it is flushed: copied as a new run
appended to runs (oldest first) and cleared. get looks in the
memtable, then runs newest to oldest; the first entry found decides
(a tombstone means empty). compact merges all runs into one, newer
entries winning, drops tombstones, and leaves zero runs if nothing is
alive; the memtable is untouched. scan(from, toExclusive) returns
live "key=value" strings in key order, merged across every level.

    limit 2: put(a,1) put(b,2)  → 1 run      delete(a) → get(a) empty
    scan("a", "c")              → [a=1, b=2]  (before the delete)

hint: a delete must leave something behind, or older runs win.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
A log-structured merge tree (LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase) never
updates a file in place. Writes go to a small sorted in-memory table;
when it fills, it is written out whole as an immutable sorted run
(an SSTable), and the memtable starts empty. Writes stay cheap and
sequential; the price is paid on reads and in background compaction.
A read therefore looks in the newest place first: memtable, then runs
from newest to oldest, and the FIRST entry found is the answer, even
if that entry is a tombstone. That is why delete must write a marker
instead of removing anything: the old value still sits in an older
run, and only a newer tombstone can hide it. Removing the key from
the memtable alone would make the old value reappear.
Compaction merges runs oldest-first into one map, so newer entries
overwrite older ones, and only then drops tombstones: with every run
merged nothing older is left for a tombstone to hide. (Real systems
compacting only SOME runs must keep tombstones, which is a classic
source of "deleted data came back" bugs.)
Optional<String> as the stored value gives the tombstone a type:
Optional.empty() is "deleted here", a missing key is "not here".

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** MVCC · snapshot isolation · commit timestamps · write conflicts  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Finish Mvcc, a multi-version store. begin() snapshots at the last
commit timestamp (0 before any). write/delete buffer in tx.writes
(delete = null). read returns tx's own buffered write if any, else the
value of the newest version with commitTs <= tx.startTs (null if none
or deleted). commit: a finished tx → IllegalStateException; any key
in tx.writes with a version committed AFTER tx.startTs →
ConflictException naming the key, nothing written; otherwise append a
Version per written key stamped ++lastCommitTs and return it. Either
way the tx is finished. gc(horizon): per key, keep the newest version
with commitTs <= horizon and every newer one; drop the rest; return
how many were dropped.

    a = begin(); b = begin(); write(a, x, 1); commit(a) → 1
    read(b, x) → null          write(b, x, 2); commit(b) → Conflict

hint: a snapshot is just a timestamp; a version is just (ts, value).
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
Multi-version concurrency control (PostgreSQL, Oracle, InnoDB) lets
readers and writers stop blocking each other by never overwriting:
each commit appends a NEW version stamped with its commit timestamp.
A transaction remembers the timestamp it started at and reads, for
each key, the newest version whose commitTs <= startTs. Later commits
exist but are invisible to it, so its reads repeat exactly. A delete
is just a version whose value is null, so a snapshot from before the
delete still sees the value.
Writes are buffered privately (read-your-own-writes checks the buffer
first) and become versions only at commit. The commit check is "first
committer wins": if any key I wrote has a version committed after my
snapshot, someone changed it under me and I must abort, writing
nothing. Keys I only read are not checked; that gap is exactly write
skew, the anomaly that separates snapshot isolation from serializable.
Garbage collection is where people lose data: for each key keep the
newest version at or below the horizon (the oldest live snapshot
still reads it) and everything newer; only versions older than that
one are unreachable. Dropping everything <= horizon breaks that
snapshot.

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** CRDTs · G-counter · last-writer-wins · idempotent merge  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Three replicas count page views while the network is split, then
gossip their states in any order, any number of times. Finish the
grow-only counter GCounter: increment(node, by) adds to that node's
slot (by < 1 → IllegalArgumentException); value() is the sum of all
slots; merge(other) returns a NEW counter whose slot for each node is
the larger of the two (neither input changes, nor shares its map).
Then write merge(a, b) for LwwRegister: the higher timestamp wins; on
a tie the register whose node id is larger (String.compareTo) wins,
so every replica picks the same one.

    x = {a:5, b:1}   y = {a:3, b:4}   x.merge(y) → {a:5, b:4}, value 9
    merge((tea,10,n1), (cake,10,n2))  → (cake,10,n2)

hint: gossip repeats itself; merging a state twice must be harmless.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
Replicas that accept writes while cut off from each other need a merge
that always agrees, whatever order the gossip arrives in and however
many times it is repeated. A CRDT gets that by making merge
commutative, associative and idempotent. The grow-only counter does it
by giving every node its own slot that only that node increments;
merge takes the per-node MAXIMUM and the value is the sum of slots.
The tempting wrong merge is adding the two counters: merging the same
state twice (which gossip does all the time) would count it twice.
Max is idempotent: max(x, x) = x.
merge returns a new counter and copies its inputs' maps, so a replica
never shares mutable state with the one it merged from.
A last-writer-wins register keeps the write with the higher timestamp.
Equal timestamps are the trap: "keep mine" makes two replicas each
keep their own value forever. Breaking ties by a total order every
replica agrees on (here the larger node id) makes merge(a, b) and
merge(b, a) identical. LWW is simple but lossy: the losing concurrent
write is silently discarded, which is why vector clocks (exercise 06)
exist.

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** vector clocks · happens-before · concurrency · siblings  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A Dynamo-style store must tell "this write replaced that one" from
"these two writes never saw each other". Finish the immutable VClock:
tick(node) returns a copy with node's counter + 1; merge(other)
returns a copy holding each node's maximum; compare(other) returns
EQUAL (all counters equal), BEFORE (all <= and one <), AFTER (the
mirror), or CONCURRENT (some < and some >). A node missing from a
clock counts as 0. Then write reconcile(versions): drop every version
whose clock is BEFORE another version's clock, and of versions with
EQUAL clocks keep only the first; keep the rest in input order.

    {a:1}      vs {a:1, b:1}  → BEFORE
    {a:2}      vs {a:1, b:1}  → CONCURRENT
    reconcile[{a:1}, {a:2}, {a:1,b:1}] → [{a:2}, {a:1,b:1}]

hint: compare over the union of both clocks' nodes.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
Wall clocks on different machines disagree, so "later timestamp wins"
(exercise 05) can throw away a write that nobody had seen. A vector
clock records causality instead: one counter per node, ticked by that
node on each write it makes, and merged (per-node max) when a node
learns another's state. Then x happened before y exactly when every
counter of x is <= y's and at least one is smaller. If each clock has
a counter the other lacks, neither saw the other: the writes are
CONCURRENT, and only the application can merge them (Dynamo's
shopping cart keeps both as "siblings").
compare walks the union of both key sets, treating a missing node as
0. The classic slip is iterating only this clock's keys, which makes
{a:1} look equal to {a:1, b:1}. Another is answering BEFORE as soon
as one counter is smaller, without checking that none is larger.
reconcile keeps a version unless some other version is strictly
AFTER it (that one already includes it), and keeps only the first of
several EQUAL versions. What survives is the set of concurrent
siblings, in input order.
Clocks are immutable values: tick and merge return new clocks, so a
clock attached to a stored version can never change behind it.

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** leases · leader election · fencing tokens · injected clocks  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Elect a leader with a lease, the way etcd and ZooKeeper do. A lease
taken at time t is live while now < t + ttl. tryAcquire(node): if the
lease is live and held by another node → empty; if live and held by
node → extend it to now + ttl, same token; otherwise node takes it
with a NEW fencing token (1, 2, 3, ...) expiring at now + ttl.
renew(node, token) extends to now + ttl only if the lease is live, is
node's, and token is its current one; else false and nothing changes.
release(node, token) ends the lease immediately under the same match;
otherwise it does nothing. leader() is the holder while live.
FencedStore.write(token, value) rejects (false) a token lower than the
highest it has accepted; equal or higher tokens are appended.

    ttl 100: t=0 acquire(A) → 1   t=50 acquire(B) → empty
             t=100 acquire(B) → 2   write(1, ...) after write(2) → false

hint: time comes only from the clock you were given.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
A lease is a lock with an expiry: whoever holds it is leader until
acquiredAt + ttl, and must renew before then. If the leader crashes,
nobody has to detect it; the lease simply runs out and another node
takes over. (ZooKeeper sessions, etcd leases, Kubernetes Lease
objects and Chubby all work this way.) The boundary matters: the
lease is live while now < expiresAt, so at exactly expiresAt it is
gone, and acquire, renew and leader() must all agree on that.
Renewing an expired lease is the classic bug: the old leader wakes up
from a long pause, renews, and now two nodes believe they lead.
Expiry alone cannot prevent that, because the paused node does not
know time passed. The fix lives in the STORAGE: each new acquisition
gets a larger fencing token, every write carries it, and the store
rejects tokens lower than the highest it has seen. A deposed leader's
late write then bounces, however confused it is. Equal tokens pass:
the current leader writes many times.
The clock is a LongSupplier so tests move time by hand; with
System.currentTimeMillis() this would need real sleeps and would
still be flaky.

javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.instructions:
**Concepts:** two-phase commit · coordinator log · presumed abort · recovery  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Commit one transaction across several databases: all or none. Finish
Coordinator. run(tx): log "tx BEGIN"; ask each participant to prepare,
in list order, stopping at the first vote that is not YES; log the
decision "tx COMMIT" (every vote YES) or "tx ABORT" BEFORE telling
anyone; then send commit to every participant, or abort only to those
that voted YES. A commit/abort call that throws is skipped (carry on
with the rest) and the decision stands; if no call threw, log
"tx DONE". recover(): for each tx in the log without DONE, in BEGIN
order: if no decision was logged, log "tx ABORT" (presumed abort);
send the decision to EVERY participant; log "tx DONE" if no call
threw. Return the ids of those transactions.

    votes YES, NO, YES → prepare p1, prepare p2, abort p1 → ABORTED
    log [t9 BEGIN]: recover() → [t9]; abort to all; + t9 ABORT, t9 DONE

hint: the log line comes first; messages can always be sent again.
javabootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency/.explanation:
Two-phase commit makes several databases agree on one outcome. Phase
one asks everyone "can you commit?"; a YES is a promise (the
participant has made the change durable and will not back out). Any
NO, or silence, dooms the transaction, so asking the rest is wasted
work. Phase two tells everyone the decision.
The decision is real the moment it is written to the coordinator's
log, and that write must happen BEFORE the first commit message. If
the coordinator sent commits first and crashed, the log would hold no
decision, recovery would presume abort, and the participants that had
already committed would disagree with the rest forever.
After the decision, failures change nothing: a participant that is
down simply has not heard yet. The coordinator keeps going, skips the
DONE record, and recovery re-sends the decision until every call
succeeds; that is why participants must treat a repeated commit or
abort as a no-op. Recovery sends to EVERY participant, because the
log does not say who voted YES. A transaction with BEGIN but no
decision crashed during phase one; nobody can have committed, so
aborting it is safe ("presumed abort").
The weakness to remember: a participant that voted YES is stuck
holding locks until the coordinator answers. That blocking is why
sagas (module 12) exist.
